rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and makes the missing proof do actual work. Its strongest line, “The story is the number, not the feature,” correctly turns the 10% fee into a reporter-shaped platform-economics angle. B has the same good skeleton, but it starts decorating with unsupplied context like “Epic v. Apple, Substack's 10%, Patreon's tiers” and overreaches with “Discord turns 200M users into a payments business,” which is exactly how a decent pitch gets gutted on first edit.
gaps_in_A: “the fee comparison is Discord's own framing” overclaims slightly; the update gives the comparison, but not proof that Discord itself is framing the launch that way.
“early adopters are new and unreported” assumes press status the update does not supply. New, yes. Unreported, not proven.
“The community server becomes the creator's paywall” is a useful trend wrapper, but it still needs outside market comparison before it deserves priority over the cleaner take-rate angle.
gaps_in_B: “Epic v. Apple, Substack's 10%, Patreon's tiers” brings in named context not supplied in the update. Maybe true, maybe useful, but blind judging does not reward freelancing.
“Discord turns 200M users into a payments business” abuses the MAU number. Monthly active users are not paying subscribers, eligible server owners, or payment volume.
“Discord, Patreon, Twitch, Geneva” invents a competitor set the update did not give. If you want that comparison, earn it with sourced take rates and product mechanics.
“moving from advertising and one-off tips toward owner-run recurring subscriptions” is a trend claim without supplied evidence. It sounds smart until a reporter asks, “Says who?”
